title: Batched allocation patterns and memory-replay playbook
content:
Summary:

This is a working playbook for diagnosing and reproducing OOMs and high watermarks that appear only under batched inference workloads. Focus is on allocation pattern interactions between variable-length requests, per-request KV cache usage, and the serving runtime's workspace lifecycle. The key idea: capture allocation/release timelines, replay them in isolation, and iterate on mitigation strategies (pooling, pre-reserve, alignment/packing) until the peak memory shape changes predictably.

Background / why this is different:
- We have several fragmentation/OOM incidents where single-model latency+throughput are fine, but latency spikes when many short and long sequences are mixed in the same batch pool.
- Hypothesis: interleaved allocations from variable sequence lengths and on-demand KV cache growth create many mid-sized free holes. CUDA's allocator behavior + alignment (256B/512B) amplifies this into reaching device memory high-watermarks even when total live bytes are modest.
- Unlike simple leaks, this is allocation topology — "where" allocations occur and in what temporal order — that prevents reuse and causes the effective usable memory to drop.

What we observe (empirical):
- Allocation histogram shows a bimodal distribution: many small allocations (512B–8KB) and many medium allocations (64KB–2MB). Medium allocations come from KV cache segments and workspace for long sequences.
- Time-sliced allocation timeline (nsys + simple tracer) shows that medium allocations often occur between many small allocations (e.g., short requests filling slots then a long request expands KV cache). The long allocation frees later but the small allocations have moved on (different lifetimes), leaving holes.
- Peak RSS (device memory) often occurs during short bursts where many allocations attempt to grow; once the long request completes the device still reports high fragmentation and subsequent requests OOM.
- Free-list blowup: seen by instrumenting allocator stats (if using custom allocator). Default CUDA allocator may return memory to OS asynchronously; cudaMalloc/cudaFree patterns matter.

Quick profiling checklist (what to collect first):
1) nsys timeline for a representative failure run. Command: 
   nsys profile --stats=true --output=batch-frag --trace=cuda,cudnn -t cuda,cudnn --sample=none --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi --force-overwrite true -- python3 load_test.py
2) Lightweight allocation tracer: LD_PRELOAD wrapper capturing cudaMalloc/cudaFree/cudaMallocAsync (if used) and record size, ptr, timestamp, stack (3 frames), and logical tags (model_id, batch_slot, seq_len).
3) Heap histograms: periodic samples of cudaMemGetInfo and the allocator internal counters (if using cuMemAlloc/third-party allocator hooks).
4) Per-request KV cache growth metrics: track kv_cache_bytes before/after for each request.

Repro recipe (deterministic replay):
- Stage 1: Record mode. Run a synthetic driver that replays traffic at various mixes (e.g., 80% short seq_len=16, 20% long seq_len=1024) and record all allocations/releases with relative timing. The trace should include: allocation size, owner tag (batch slot, request id), and order.
- Stage 2: Isolated replay harness. Build a small C++/CUDA harness that replays the exact sequence of cudaMalloc/cudaFree calls with original timing (or aggressive timings) on a dedicated GPU. This removes higher-level runtime concurrency and isolates allocator behavior.
- Stage 3: Variant replays. Modify replay to: (a) coalesce adjacent small frees into single free (b) change alignment to 256/512/4096 (prepend extra padding) (c) reserve medium slabs before starting. Compare peak usage and fragmentation map.

Practical experiments to try (priority order):
1) Synthetic mix sweep: run replays for mixes {100% short, 90/10, 80/20, 50/50, 100% long} and measure peak device free and fragmentation metric (max_allocable_single_block from probing).
2) Per-model workspace pooling: pre-allocate a workspace pool equal to 1.1x observed max per-model workspace (for the long sequences) and carve small fixed-size arenas inside. Run mix to see if fragmentation disappears.
3) Power-of-two slab allocator experiment: change allocator to round medium allocations to power-of-two classes and use segregated lists (in the replay harness only) — measure reclaim behavior.
4) KV cache sharding: instead of a single contiguous grow, try split KV into per-batch-slot segments pre-reserved so growth is limited to reserved buckets.
5) Eviction policy test: force early eviction of cold KV segments when free memory drops below threshold and observe tradeoffs on latency vs OOM frequency.

Observed metrics to record for each experiment:
- Peak allocated device bytes (cudaMemGetInfo before/after loop).
- Largest contiguous free region (probe by binary-search allocating descending sizes until fail).
- Number of allocation failures and where they happened (stack tags).
- Allocation churn: allocations/sec and frees/sec by size bucket.

Short-term mitigations (fast to deploy):
- Warmup reservation: on model load or pool startup do a single long-run synthetic request to pre-grow KV cache, then release and keep reserved arenas for reuse. This reduces on-demand mid-run expansion.
- Per-batch-slot per-request reuse: ensure workspace tensors are allocated from an LRU reusable pool keyed by size class and batch_slot.
- Conservative max sequence length cap for mixed-batch pools: funnel long sequences into a separate capacity pool so they don't interleave with short requests.

Longer-term mitigations (architectural):
- Integrate a power-of-two slab allocator into the serving runtime for workspace + KV cache allocations. This reduces internal fragmentation at the cost of some external slack. Document decimals for ROI for typical token distributions.
- Add an allocator-visible tagging API so we can identify "evictable" vs "pinned" allocations. Allows runtime to compact by freeing evictable blocks first.
- Support model-level workspace reservations in scheduling logic: the scheduler should avoid co-locating many long-seq requests in the same placement unit unless capacity reserved.

Instrumentation tips / gotchas:
- cudaMemGetInfo is cheap relative to work; sample it around key life-cycle boundaries.
- nsys provides excellent timeline but opaque ptr addresses; combine with LD_PRELOAD tracer to map addresses to logical owners.
- Beware that cudaMallocAsync (on newer drivers) defers actual device allocations; behavior under async allocator differs significantly from immediate cudaMalloc. Test both code paths.
- Alignment/padding: some internal CUDA datastructures prefer 256B; a small change to alignment can flip which free-list bucket an allocation uses and therefore fragmentation behaviour.

Open questions / next steps:
- Which allocator are we using in prod for the failing fleet? (driver default vs jemalloc-like layer vs custom pool)
- Can we cheaply add tagging in the runtime (request id, model id, batch slot) on allocations? This helps triage.
- How do multi-GPU and peer-to-peer allocations affect fragmentation patterns under our routing policies?

Appendix: quick LD_PRELOAD trace idea (sketch)
- Build a tiny wrapper intercepting cudaMalloc/cudaFree with C symbols and log: ts, tid, size, returned ptr, backtrace[3], and environment tags (MODEL_ID, BATCH_SLOT, SEQ_LEN). Write to ring buffer file for performance, then post-process into replay script.
- Example log line: 
  2025-02-10T12:01:23.123Z | tid=2341 | alloc | 65536 | 0x7f8a1b2c0000 | model=alex-anders/7b | batch_slot=3 | seq_len=1024

Replay harness considerations:
- The replay program should support speed-up mode (ignore original delays) and timed mode (respect original inter-arrival). Speed-up helps test high-concurrency stress.
- Provide options to change alignment and to pre-allocate fixed slabs to see effects.

Notes from initial runs (Ravi/Maya):
- Replay of a 80/20 mix reduced peak by ~18% when using pre-reserved 1.2x workspace slabs.
- Power-of-two rounding in harness reduced number of free-list entries by ~30% but increased baseline by ~6% memory overhead.

If you run any of these experiments, paste the trace file and the nsys .qdrep into the /shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/investigations/batch-frag/ folder (we don't have write here so just ping in Slack #eng-runtime). Include the replay script used.

Questions for design review: is 6% steady-state overhead acceptable if it avoids intermittent OOMs and reduces operational incidents by >50%?

Next owner: Ravi to land capture scaffolding; Maya to run synthetic mix sweep and fill the experiment table with metrics. I will iterate on a minimal slab allocator prototype for the runtime.
